passage: Note from the class teacher, after the science test. Payal stayed at her desk when the others left and asked to speak to me. She said that during question 7 she had seen Vandana's answer from where she sat, and no one was looking. "I wanted those marks so much," she said. "But then I thought, if I write that, the answer isn't mine." She had written her own answer, unsure and probably wrong. She still looked a little sorry about the lost mark. I told her I was glad she came to talk, and we agreed on a short revision plan for the unit on electricity. She left with a lighter step.

qa.q: During which question did Payal see Vandana's answer?
What did Payal want, and what did she worry about, while she looked at question 7?
qa.a: She wanted the marks, but she also wanted the answer to be her own; afterwards she still looked a little sorry about the lost mark.

qa.q: What small step would help Payal with the unit on electricity?
qa.a: A short revision plan with the teacher, so that her own answers get stronger.

qa.q: How might Vandana feel if Vandana later heard what Payal did?
qa.a: Vandana might be surprised and maybe respect Payal for it; the note does not say Vandana ever found out.

grounding: Illustrates a child tempted by a friend's visible answer who chooses to write her own.

passage: 'Parul, you want to know if I ever cheated? I nearly did, once. Your Pooja Bua was in Class 5, sitting in the exam hall with the fan clattering. I was stuck on the last sum. The girl next to me, Meena, had left her paper right at the edge of the desk, and the answer was there, circled. The invigilator was dozing in her chair. Nobody would ever know. Part of me wanted those five marks so badly. Another part pictured showing Amma my paper and knowing it wasn't really mine. I turned my face to the wall and tried the sum again. I got it wrong. I still remember that wrong answer, and I'm prouder of it than of any right one.'

qa.q: How many marks was the last sum worth?
What was young Pooja feeling when she saw Meena's answer?
qa.a: Tempted and torn; part of her badly wanted the marks, and part wanted to be proud of her own work.

qa.q: What choice in the story built young Pooja's strength?
qa.a: Turning her face to the wall and trying the sum herself, even though she got it wrong.

qa.q: How might Meena have felt if she had seen Pooja copying?
qa.a: Uneasy or let down that her work was taken without asking.

grounding: An aunt recalls being tempted by a classmate's answer when nobody was watching, and choosing honesty over marks.

passage: Five minutes left in the geography exam, and Sir had been called out to the office. The room went buzzy with whispers. Deepak was stuck on the map question: which river flows through Guwahati? Tenzin's paper lay open on the next desk, turned towards him. Deepak's heart thudded. Nobody was looking. He could glance, just once. Five marks. But then he'd walk home knowing, and Tenzin would never know what he'd taken. Deepak shut his eyes and pictured the map on the classroom wall, the big blue snake curling through Assam. He wrote Brahmaputra, not quite sure. When Sir came back, the bell rang. Walking out, Tenzin said, 'Brahmaputra, right?' Deepak grinned. He had got it himself, and his chest felt clean.

qa.q: Why had Sir left the room?
qa.a: He had been called out to the office.

qa.q: What was Deepak feeling when he saw Tenzin's open paper?
qa.a: Tempted and nervous, his heart thudding, pulled between wanting five marks and wanting to be proud of himself.

qa.q: What did Deepak do instead of glancing?
qa.a: He shut his eyes, pictured the classroom map, and worked out the answer himself.

qa.q: What would change if Deepak had glanced at Tenzin's paper?
qa.a: He might have got the same answer, but he would have walked home guilty instead of with a clean chest.

grounding: With the teacher out of the room, a boy is tempted by a friend's open paper and chooses to work the answer out himself.
